project_scope.selection_mode: Central Texas family-first recognition module with Stillingia canonical anchor and project-pool genus roadmap
project_scope.note: Teach the broad Euphorbiaceae architecture first, then route the learner into genus-level patterns. Stillingia texana is the current canonical local anchor. Euphorbia, Croton, Acalypha, and Tragia species work remains in separate scout/deep-review lanes and is not silently promoted here.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: Do not start with latex. First look for very small unisexual flowers and a superior ovary/fruit built on a usually 3-carpellate plan. A dry 3-part capsule or schizocarp separating around a persistent central column is the strongest broad-family field confirmation.
family_diagnostics.vegetative: Habit and leaves are extremely variable. Leaves are often alternate and simple; stipules, petiole/blade glands, latex, and distinctive hairs are useful clues in many genera but none is a safe family-wide requirement.
family_diagnostics.reproductive: Flowers are unisexual and usually small or highly reduced. The ovary is superior and commonly 3-locular/3-carpellate, with one ovule per locule. Male and female flowers may occur in separate portions of the same inflorescence.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Usually a dry dehiscent capsule/schizocarp. The cocci commonly separate from a persistent central columella; one seed is typically produced per locule.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Family first: tiny unisexual flowers + superior usually 3-part ovary/fruit. Genus second: cyathium, stellate hairs, stinging hairs, pistillate bracts, or Stillingia's spike/gynobase architecture. Treat latex as supporting evidence only.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: 3-part ovary/fruit → reduced unisexual flowers → choose a genus pattern → confirm with genus-specific structures
visual_lesson.intro: The spurge family is easier when you stop searching for one universal leaf or one universal flower. Learn the three-part reproductive plan first, then sort the unknown into one of several very different local genus patterns.

steps.title: 1 · Start with the three-part reproductive plan
steps.look_for: A superior ovary or capsule with a three-part outline; when mature, the fruit commonly separates into sections around a central column.
steps.why_it_matters: This is more broadly transferable across Euphorbiaceae than latex, leaf shape, or the Euphorbia cyathium.

steps.title: 2 · Notice how reduced the flowers are
steps.photo_role: small unisexual flowers on one inflorescence
steps.look_for: Separate male and female flowers that are small, inconspicuous, and often arranged in different zones of the same inflorescence.
steps.why_it_matters: Tiny unisexual flowers plus the three-part ovary/fruit strongly reinforce the family call.

steps.title: 3 · Euphorbia door: find the cyathium
steps.look_for: A cup-like involucre with nectar glands surrounding extremely reduced male flowers and a central female flower. It looks like one flower but is an inflorescence.
steps.why_it_matters: The cyathium is one of the fastest genus-level recognitions in botany, but it belongs to Euphorbia—not to the whole family.

steps.title: 4 · Croton door: inspect the hairs
steps.photo_role: leaf/stem macro showing stellate or scale-like trichomes
steps.look_for: Star-shaped or scale-like hairs, often giving the plant a gray, silvery, or rough appearance; many Croton also place pistillate flowers lower and staminate flowers higher in a raceme or spike.
steps.why_it_matters: Croton hair architecture is a high-value genus clue and is much more useful than trying to memorize overall plant shape.

steps.title: 5 · Acalypha door: read the female bracts
steps.look_for: Pistillate flowers subtended by conspicuous bracts that often enlarge as fruit develops, with styles commonly split into many narrow branches.
steps.why_it_matters: The enlarged pistillate bracts and finely divided styles give Acalypha a distinctive reproductive silhouette.

steps.title: 6 · Stinging-hair door: Tragia vs Cnidoscolus
steps.look_for: Tragia is usually a smaller herb/subshrub/vine with stinging hairs and no latex; Cnidoscolus combines stinging hairs with white latex and often deeply palmately lobed leaves and larger petaloid flowers.
steps.why_it_matters: Both can punish a careless hand, but their habit, latex, leaves, and flower size quickly split the two genera.

steps.title: 7 · Stillingia door: read the spike and the leftover base
steps.photo_role: basal pistillate / upper staminate spike + persistent gynobase
steps.look_for: One or more pistillate flowers near the base of a spikelike inflorescence, staminate clusters above, and after fruit dehiscence a persistent hardened 3-part gynobase.
steps.why_it_matters: The persistent gynobase is an especially strong Stillingia character and gives the family lesson a real Edwards Plateau anchor.

comparisons.title: Euphorbiaceae vs Phyllanthaceae
comparisons.rule: Both were historically lumped in a broad spurge family. In modern Euphorbiaceae, the ovary characteristically has one ovule per locule; Phyllanthaceae characteristically has two. Latex and leaf/petiole glands also favor Euphorbiaceae but are not universal.

comparisons.title: Euphorbiaceae vs Apocynaceae
comparisons.rule: Milky latex can occur in both. Euphorbiaceae commonly combines tiny unisexual flowers with a superior usually 3-carpellate capsule; Apocynaceae more often has conspicuous fused corollas and a 2-carpel gynoecium, with milkweeds adding pollinia/gynostegium characters.

comparisons.title: Euphorbiaceae vs Urticaceae
comparisons.rule: Stinging hairs alone do not mean nettle family. Tragia and Cnidoscolus can sting; confirm Euphorbiaceae with unisexual floral architecture and the superior usually 3-part ovary/capsule.

comparisons.title: Euphorbia vs the rest of Euphorbiaceae
comparisons.rule: A cyathium points strongly to Euphorbia, but Croton, Acalypha, Tragia, Cnidoscolus, Stillingia and other family members do not use the Euphorbia cyathium architecture.

visual_lesson.caveat: The family is morphologically diverse. Latex, stipules, glands, stellate hairs and three-lobed fruit are common clues rather than universal absolutes. Use several reproductive characters together, then switch to genus-specific traits.
